name: Hole volume
seoDesc: Hole volume: work out radius from the depth and the volume. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Hole volume calculator the depth and the volume and it returns radius. It suits a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Hole volume calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hole volume calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports radius in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the depth (Circular hole), the volume (Circular hole), the depth (Rectangular hole) and the width.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hole volume calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Radius=the square root of (volume ÷ depth) ÷ the square root of (PI)
Length=volume ÷ (depth × width)
Waste=required concrete (circular hole) ÷ (volume × quantity of posts) − 1
Waste=required concrete (rectangular hole) ÷ (volume × quantity of posts) − 1
Radius=(1 ÷ 2) × diameter

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Depth = 30 cm, Volume = 10 m³ and Waste = 7 %. The calculator returns Radius = 0.3257 cm and Diameter = 0.6515 cm.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Radius = 0.3257 cm and Diameter = 0.6515 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Depth = 30 cm and Volume = 10 m³.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters

  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hole volume calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the depth and the volume — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hole volume calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns radius, derived from the depth and the volume. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hole volume calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the depth and the volume, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter depth (Circular hole) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Depth (Circular hole) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Radius = 0.3257 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Hole volume calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
